newsitem.title: JAPAN: Former Fed official says US policy change unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Former Fed official says US policy change unlikely.

text.p: The U.S. economy is in an ideal state and there seems to be little reason for the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy soon, an influential former official of the powerful Fed said in Tokyo on Friday.

Although Alan Blinder, formerly the Fed's vice chairman, declined to predict his former colleagues' future decision-making, he said: "If I were still at the Fed, I would be wanting to hold (interest rates) where they are."
Fears have emerged recently in U.S. financial markets that the Fed may tighten credit at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on the back of strong economic data.
The FOMC is to meet on February 4 and 5.
But Blinder, now a professor at Princeton University in New Jersey, said it was not urgent for the Fed to raise rates just for the sake of achieving short-term price stability.

"While it would be better probably to have 1-1/2 percent inflation than 2-3/4 percent, the social cost of that small difference, as long as inflation is stable, is quite small," he said. He was in Tokyo on the last leg of an Asian speaking tour.
He also reiterated his long-held view that regarding inflation, the Fed could wait until the next recession, which would bring down inflation.
"We know that whenever the next recession comes, although it's not on the horizon, it will knock a point or two off the inflation rate," Blinder said.

On the issue of U.S. stock prices, which have been hitting record highs recently, Blinder said they now pose a downside risk to the economy and it would not be a surprise to see a substantial drop in the Dow Industrials anytime now.
"It wouldn't be a big surprise any day, any week, to see a substantial drop," Blinder said, adding that the Dow could fall several hundred points, or between five and 10 percent.
The Dow Industrials set a new closing high on Thursday, finishing 38 points or 0.57 percent higher at 6,765.
Blinder also played down views that the recent rise of the dollar would hurt U.S. exports.
He said the dollar's movement against currencies other than the yen had not been that dramatic and in trade-weighted average terms, its movement had been fairly modest.
"So it is a small negative for U.S. export performance but not a major one." he said.
He added that the rise of the dollar against the yen was mostly a normalisation of an excessively strong yen.
